text: Storms, onshore wind, heavy runoff and El Niño conditions can all raise the Bay above the predicted tide.

text: “Average high tide” is Mean Higher High Water (MHHW): the average of each day’s highest tide at the NOAA tide gauge in {station}, {mhhw} ft NAVD88. Tides above it reach farther onto low shorelines, marshes and trails. Based on NOAA tide measurements, NOAA’s model forecast and the predicted (astronomical) tide.
shown_on: home page (Bay tides card, small print)
notes: {station} and {mhhw} are filled in from tide_stations.csv

text: MHHW (Mean Higher High Water) is the average height of the highest tide each day. Tides above it reach farther up shorelines, marshes and low-lying areas than usual.
shown_on: Tides page (explainer)

text: NOAA forecast is model guidance from NOAA's San Francisco Bay Operational Forecast System: the water level at this gauge including wind, air pressure and river flow, about 2 days ahead, updated 4 times a day. It is not an official forecast; NWS advisories take precedence.
shown_on: Tides page (explainer), kiosk Bay Tides tap screen

text: Predicted tides come from NOAA and don't include storm surge, wind or runoff.
shown_on: Tides page (small print), kiosk Bay Tides tap screen

text: King Tide dates from San Mateo County Emergency Management, “Tide days of concern, Oct 2026 to Apr 2027.” They are astronomical tide predictions for NOAA’s San Francisco gauge (9414290) and don’t include weather. Redwood City tides usually run higher than San Francisco, and storms, wind and runoff can add more, so check the Redwood City predictions and NWS alerts for the actual forecast.
